summary: Extends Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (RFC 7683) with a Peer Overload report type. The first use case is handling overload of a Diameter Agent. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: When a helper in a chain gets swamped, it can tell its neighbors, so they send it less work.

questions: what is a diameter peer overload report
subtitle: Lets an overloaded Diameter agent tell its neighbours to send less traffic, using a new Peer Overload report.

tldr.problem: The base Diameter overload solution (RFC 7683) handles overloaded clients and servers, but not the case where a Diameter Agent in the middle becomes overloaded.
tldr.mechanism: A new Peer Overload report type, announced with the OC_PEER_REPORT feature bit and tied to a SourceID AVP, lets an agent ask its direct peers to reduce traffic, preferably by diverting it elsewhere.
tldr.outcome: Reacting nodes first try to divert abated requests to other peers and throttle only what cannot be diverted. The report type is generic enough to be used for other overload scenarios.

today: RFC 8581 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2019. It updates RFC 7683 and has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: Overload at Diameter Agents
sections.content:
This RFC extends the Diameter Overload Indication Conveyance (DOIC) solution from RFC 7683. That base specification deals with overloaded Diameter endpoints (a client or a server) and aims to handle abatement as close to the source of the traffic as feasible.

A Diameter Agent, which provides relay, proxy, redirect or translation services, can also be asked to handle more traffic than it was configured for. This document defines a new Peer Overload report type to communicate that. It is written generically so it can serve other overload scenarios too, and it works with the loss abatement algorithm of RFC 7683 and is expected to work with algorithms defined in other extensions.
sections.eli5: A messenger in the middle of a chain can get too much to carry, just like the people at either end. This memo gives that messenger a way to say so.

sections.title: Deployment Cases
sections.content:
The RFC walks through several layouts. With a single agent between client and server(s), an overload report from the agent is handled like an overloaded directly connected server. Since there is no alternative route, the abated traffic is throttled and the client sends an error response to the originator of the request.

With redundant agents, the client has connections to two agents, either primary and secondary or both actively used. The client should move the requested amount of traffic to the non-overloaded agent. For example, if an agent asks for a reduction of 10 percent, the client sends 10 percent of the traffic that would have gone to it through the other agent. If both agents report overload, the client may need to reduce total traffic.

With agent chains, such as agents between administrative domains, the previous-hop agent handles the overload of the next one. It diverts traffic if it can, and otherwise throttles using the error responses defined in the base DOIC specification.

The RFC also expects that endpoints could send peer reports, for example when the rate algorithm (RFC 8582) is used hop by hop.
sections.eli5: If one helper is swamped and you have another one, you hand some work to the second. If you have only one helper, you have to turn some requests away.

sections.title: Announcing Peer-Report Support
sections.content:
A DOIC node that supports the OC_PEER_REPORT feature MUST set that bit in the OC-Feature-Vector AVP of the OC-Supported-Features AVP in every request it sends. It MUST also include a SourceID AVP with its own DiameterIdentity. An agent relaying such a request replaces the received SourceID with its own.

On receiving a request, a supporting node records in transaction state whether the peer it came from supports the feature. The peer counts as supporting it only if the feature bit is set and the SourceID matches the DiameterIdentity of the peer that sent the request. A reporting node strips any SourceID when relaying an answer.

When answering a supporting peer, the reporting node MUST indicate support, insert its SourceID, and insert an OC-Peer-Algo AVP naming the abatement algorithm it wants reacting nodes to use if it later sends a Peer Overload report. Peer reports are only sent to peers that support the feature.
sections.eli5: Neighbors first show each other a name tag and say they know how to handle this kind of message. Only then will a swamped helper send its call for help.

sections.title: Overload Control State and Report Handling
sections.content:
A reacting node keeps a peer-report OCS (overload control state) entry per supported application for each peer it sends requests to, identified by the Application-ID and the peer's DiameterIdentity. An entry holds the sequence number, the time of expiry, the selected abatement algorithm and any algorithm-specific data such as the reduction percentage. A reporting node SHOULD keep its own state, and MUST keep a separate entry per peer if it sends different abatement contents to each peer.

When an OC-OLR AVP of type PEER-REPORT arrives, the reacting node MUST check that its SourceID matches the peer that delivered the response. If not, it MUST ignore the report. This guards against peer reports inserted by mistake or maliciously.

For a matching existing entry, a report with a greater sequence number updates it, and one with a sequence number less than or equal to the stored one is silently ignored. A report for a new condition creates a new entry. A validity duration of zero marks the entry as expired, and an answer with no OC-OLR AVP means no change.
sections.eli5: Each neighbor keeps a note saying how much work to send to which helper and for how long. A newer note replaces an older one, and notes from strangers are ignored.

sections.title: Reacting-Node Behavior
sections.content:
A reacting node MUST be able to handle several Overload reports in one message, such as Host, Realm and Peer reports. When both a Host or Realm report and a peer report apply, it handles the Host or Realm throttling first. Messages that survive then go through peer-report abatement, and the node SHOULD take into account the messages already throttled, to avoid traffic oscillations.

If a request matches an active OCS entry, abatement applies. For peer reports, the preferred treatment is diversion: the node SHOULD try to divert requests to other peers. If there is not enough capacity, it MUST throttle what is needed to fit the capacity of the peers able to take the traffic. A throttling agent MUST send an appropriate error response as defined in RFC 7683. An agent MUST strip the Peer-Report OC-OLR AVP from messages it forwards.

When an entry expires or has a validity duration of zero, meaning the reporting node has explicitly signaled the end of the overload, abatement MUST be ended in a controlled fashion.
sections.eli5: When told to send less, first try handing the extra to someone else. Only if no one can take it do you say no, and when the call for help ends you ease back to normal gradually.

sections.title: New and Changed AVPs
sections.content:
The OC_PEER_REPORT feature bit has the value 0x0000000000000010 in the OC-Feature-Vector AVP. OC-Peer-Algo (AVP code 648, type Unsigned64) announces the abatement algorithm for peer reports; the value zero is reserved and the bits reuse the algorithm feature bits of OC-Feature-Vector. SourceID (AVP code 649, type DiameterIdentity) carries the DiameterIdentity of the node that inserted the enclosing AVP.

The OC-OLR AVP gains an optional SourceID so the reacting node knows which agent generated the report. This matters when a non-supporting agent sits between the reporting and reacting nodes, because otherwise the reacting node might wrongly assume the report applied to the non-supporting node.

The new OC-Report-Type value is PEER_REPORT (2). It means the overload treatment applies to all requests bound for the identified peer. If that is not a peer of the reacting endpoint, the report is stripped and not acted on. Neither new AVP may have the V flag set.
sections.eli5: The new messages carry a name tag saying who is asking for help, so nobody mistakes the message for one from a different helper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: All the security considerations of RFC 7683 apply. The RFC adds that malicious insertion of a peer report could have a bigger impact than an endpoint report, because agents can be concentration points. Where an endpoint report affects traffic to a single server, a peer report could throttle all traffic to the Diameter network. The effect is amplified for an agent at the edge of a network that is the entry point from all other Diameter networks. The impacts and mitigations are the same as in RFC 7683.
sections.eli5: A fake call for help to a busy crossroads could stop a lot of traffic at once, so these messages must be checked.
